<h1>Building a pattern</h1>

Two walkthroughs of the trig view, each building a pattern one gesture at a
time. The first shows what the trig types do to a sequence, the second what
decides how long each note lasts. [Trigs](/documentation/MSEQ/trigs) is the reference behind
both: what every colour means and which modifier writes it.

---

## Writing a pattern, one gesture at a time

The quickest way to get a feel for the trig types is to watch a pattern grow.
Everything below happens on one sequencer in C minor (see
[Chords and scales](/documentation/MSEQ/chords-and-scales) for how key and scale are set), and
each figure changes exactly one thing from the figure before it, so you can
attribute every difference to the gesture that caused it.

**1. Plain trigs.** Start with a standard trig (no modifier held) on steps
1, 5, 9 and 13 of row 1, the bottom row, which in C minor plays C3.

<figure class="fig-pair">
<input type="radio" name="trig-01-one-note" id="trig-01-one-note-webapp" class="pick-webapp" checked>
<label for="trig-01-one-note-webapp">webapp</label>
<input type="radio" name="trig-01-one-note" id="trig-01-one-note-hardware" class="pick-hardware">
<label for="trig-01-one-note-hardware">hardware</label>
<img class="shot-webapp" src="/assets/mseq/trig-01-one-note.png" alt="A Launchpad grid with four teal pads on the bottom row, at steps 1, 5, 9 and 13, each labelled C3">
<img class="shot-hardware" src="/assets/mseq/hardware/trig-01-one-note.jpg" alt="A Launchpad grid with four teal pads on the bottom row, at steps 1, 5, 9 and 13, each labelled C3, photographed on the hardware">
</figure>

*One note, four trigs: C3 on steps 1, 5, 9 and 13.*

These fire every time round, and give you a steady spine for everything else to
hang off.

**2. A chord.** The grid is 8 rows × 16 steps, and on a synth sequencer each of the
eight rows is a note, so write the same four steps on rows 3 and 5 as well.

<figure class="fig-pair">
<input type="radio" name="trig-02-chord" id="trig-02-chord-webapp" class="pick-webapp" checked>
<label for="trig-02-chord-webapp">webapp</label>
<input type="radio" name="trig-02-chord" id="trig-02-chord-hardware" class="pick-hardware">
<label for="trig-02-chord-hardware">hardware</label>
<img class="shot-webapp" src="/assets/mseq/trig-02-chord.png" alt="The same four-step rhythm now lit on three rows, labelled C3, D#3 and G3, forming a C minor triad">
<img class="shot-hardware" src="/assets/mseq/hardware/trig-02-chord.jpg" alt="The same four-step rhythm now lit on three rows, labelled C3, D#3 and G3, forming a C minor triad, photographed on the hardware">
</figure>

*The same rhythm on three rows becomes a chord: C3, D♯3 and G3.*

Same rhythm, three rows, and you have a chord. The note labels are doing the
teaching here.

**3. Muting a trig without deleting it.** Now hold **MUTE** and press step 5
on all three rows.

<figure class="fig-pair">
<input type="radio" name="trig-03-trigmute" id="trig-03-trigmute-webapp" class="pick-webapp" checked>
<label for="trig-03-trigmute-webapp">webapp</label>
<input type="radio" name="trig-03-trigmute" id="trig-03-trigmute-hardware" class="pick-hardware">
<label for="trig-03-trigmute-hardware">hardware</label>
<img class="shot-webapp" src="/assets/mseq/trig-03-trigmute.png" alt="The same chord, with the step 5 pads changed from teal to tan on all three rows">
<img class="shot-hardware" src="/assets/mseq/hardware/trig-03-trigmute.jpg" alt="The same chord, with the step 5 pads changed from teal to tan on all three rows, photographed on the hardware">
</figure>

*Step 5 held MUTE: the trigs stay visible in tan, but stop firing.*

They remain lit up but are disabled, which is useful for paring back a busy
pattern that you might want to reprise later on.

**4. Percentage chance.** Hold **SHIFT** and press step 9 on each row. They light
green, and how pale they are tells you how likely they are to hit.

<figure class="fig-pair">
<input type="radio" name="trig-04-chance" id="trig-04-chance-webapp" class="pick-webapp" checked>
<label for="trig-04-chance-webapp">webapp</label>
<input type="radio" name="trig-04-chance" id="trig-04-chance-hardware" class="pick-hardware">
<label for="trig-04-chance-hardware">hardware</label>
<img class="shot-webapp" src="/assets/mseq/trig-04-chance.png" alt="The same chord, with the step 9 pads now green, indicating percentage-chance trigs">
<img class="shot-hardware" src="/assets/mseq/hardware/trig-04-chance.jpg" alt="The same chord, with the step 9 pads now green, indicating percentage-chance trigs, photographed on the hardware">
</figure>

*Step 9 held SHIFT: percentage-chance trigs, in green.*

The bottom knob for that sequencer on the relevant launchcontrol sets the
threshold, so you can dial the whole row from "barely there" to "always" without
touching the pattern itself. Note that SHIFT toggles a step between OFF and
percentage chance, so converting a step that is already on takes two presses.

**5. Mod chance.** Holding **REC ARM** and pressing a step cycles it through the
modulo divisions. One press on step 13 of each row puts it on MOD1.

<figure class="fig-pair">
<input type="radio" name="trig-05-mod-chance" id="trig-05-mod-chance-webapp" class="pick-webapp" checked>
<label for="trig-05-mod-chance-webapp">webapp</label>
<input type="radio" name="trig-05-mod-chance" id="trig-05-mod-chance-hardware" class="pick-hardware">
<label for="trig-05-mod-chance-hardware">hardware</label>
<img class="shot-webapp" src="/assets/mseq/trig-05-mod-chance.png" alt="The same chord, with the step 13 pads now pale pink, indicating a MOD1 conditional trig">
<img class="shot-hardware" src="/assets/mseq/hardware/trig-05-mod-chance.jpg" alt="The same chord, with the step 13 pads now pale pink, indicating a MOD1 conditional trig, photographed on the hardware">
</figure>

*Step 13 held REC ARM: MOD1, in pale pink, fires on even bars only.*

**6. Longer cycles.** Back in the grid, keep pressing **REC ARM** on a step to
walk further up the divisions. MOD2 also hits every other bar but on the odd
ones, MOD4 hits every fourth bar, MOD8 every eighth, and MOD16 once per sixteen
bar cycle. Sprinkle those on steps 12, 14 and 16 and the pattern takes the full
cycle to come round: the same sixteen steps, but never quite the same twice. The
mod divisions read as a run: pink, lilac, then three deepening blues.

**7. Inverting the condition.** Swapping mod chance for inverse mod chance on
those same steps (hold **8A**) means they now hit every time *except* the
fourth, eighth or sixteenth bar. Notice the colour changes from light blue →
blue → dark blue, to mustard → dark orange → dark red. The same accents, punched
out rather than punched in.

From here, [Euclidean overlays](/documentation/MSEQ/euclidean) will fill in the gaps
algorithmically, the [step views](/documentation/MSEQ/step-views) give each of those hits its own
length and loudness, and the [note arps](/documentation/MSEQ/note-arp) change *which* note each
trigger fires.

---

## How long is a note?

The grid says *when* a note fires. How long it then lasts is decided somewhere
else, and there are three routes to it: the step's own duty value, a held trig
across several steps, or the row's play mode. They stack, which is worth seeing in
order. Everything below is the same four-to-the-floor chord on three rows, so the
only thing changing is the length of the notes.

(In these figures the middle row is the one selected for editing, which is why its
trigs are a shade different from the other two.)

**1. A chord, with the rows muted.** Nothing sounds yet.

<figure class="fig-pair">
<input type="radio" name="4-4-muted" id="4-4-muted-webapp" class="pick-webapp" checked>
<label for="4-4-muted-webapp">webapp</label>
<input type="radio" name="4-4-muted" id="4-4-muted-hardware" class="pick-hardware">
<label for="4-4-muted-hardware">hardware</label>
<img class="shot-webapp" src="/assets/mseq/4-4-muted.png" alt="A grid with three rows of four teal trigs each, on steps 1, 5, 9 and 13, and every row button on the right unlit">
<img class="shot-hardware" src="/assets/mseq/hardware/4-4-muted.jpg" alt="A grid with three rows of four teal trigs each, on steps 1, 5, 9 and 13, and every row button on the right unlit, photographed on the hardware">
</figure>

*Twelve trigs written and not one of them playing. The row buttons down the right
are all dark, which is what muted looks like: the pattern is there, waiting.*

**2. Unmute the rows.** Press each row button.

<figure class="fig-pair">
<input type="radio" name="4-4-unmuted" id="4-4-unmuted-webapp" class="pick-webapp" checked>
<label for="4-4-unmuted-webapp">webapp</label>
<input type="radio" name="4-4-unmuted" id="4-4-unmuted-hardware" class="pick-hardware">
<label for="4-4-unmuted-hardware">hardware</label>
<img class="shot-webapp" src="/assets/mseq/4-4-unmuted.png" alt="The same three rows of trigs, now with the row buttons lit orange, and the step 1 pads washed out where the playhead sits">
<img class="shot-hardware" src="/assets/mseq/hardware/4-4-unmuted.jpg" alt="The same three rows of trigs, now with the row buttons lit orange, and the step 1 pads washed out where the playhead sits, photographed on the hardware">
</figure>

*Orange row buttons mean unmuted, and now each trig fires. How long each note
lasts is its step's duty value (see [Step values](/documentation/MSEQ/step-views)), so at the
default of one sixteenth you get four short notes to the bar. The washed-out pads
on step 1 are the playhead passing through.*

**3. Hold every trig across to the next one.** Hold **SOLO**, press a start step,
then an end step, and repeat until the bar is covered. Muted again first, because
the pattern is easier to read when nothing is moving through it.

<figure class="fig-pair">
<input type="radio" name="4-4-held-muted" id="4-4-held-muted-webapp" class="pick-webapp" checked>
<label for="4-4-held-muted-webapp">webapp</label>
<input type="radio" name="4-4-held-muted" id="4-4-held-muted-hardware" class="pick-hardware">
<label for="4-4-held-muted-hardware">hardware</label>
<img class="shot-webapp" src="/assets/mseq/4-4-held-muted.png" alt="Three rows filled right across all sixteen steps: yellow-green pads at steps 1, 5, 9 and 13, each followed by three slate pads, and every row button on the right unlit">
<img class="shot-hardware" src="/assets/mseq/hardware/4-4-held-muted.jpg" alt="Three rows filled right across all sixteen steps: yellow-green pads at steps 1, 5, 9 and 13, each followed by three slate pads, and every row button on the right unlit, photographed on the hardware">
</figure>

*Four held notes to a row now, running 1 to 4, 5 to 8, 9 to 12 and 13 to 16, so
there is no gap anywhere in the bar. The yellow-green pad is where each note
starts and the slate pads behind it are that note still sounding.*

<figure class="fig-pair">
<input type="radio" name="4-4-held-unmuted" id="4-4-held-unmuted-webapp" class="pick-webapp" checked>
<label for="4-4-held-unmuted-webapp">webapp</label>
<input type="radio" name="4-4-held-unmuted" id="4-4-held-unmuted-hardware" class="pick-hardware">
<label for="4-4-held-unmuted-hardware">hardware</label>
<img class="shot-webapp" src="/assets/mseq/4-4-held-unmuted.png" alt="The same filled pattern with the row buttons now orange and the step 1 pads washed out where the playhead sits">
<img class="shot-hardware" src="/assets/mseq/hardware/4-4-held-unmuted.jpg" alt="The same filled pattern with the row buttons now orange and the step 1 pads washed out where the playhead sits, photographed on the hardware">
</figure>

*Unmuted, and the difference from step 2 is the whole point: the same four notes
per bar, but each one lasts until the next begins instead of stopping after a
sixteenth. Nothing retriggers in between. This is legato in all but name, written
into the pattern by hand.*

**4. Or hold some and leave others short.** Held trigs are not all-or-nothing:
vary the regions and mix plain trigs in among them.

<figure class="fig-pair">
<input type="radio" name="4-4-held-ptn" id="4-4-held-ptn-webapp" class="pick-webapp" checked>
<label for="4-4-held-ptn-webapp">webapp</label>
<input type="radio" name="4-4-held-ptn" id="4-4-held-ptn-hardware" class="pick-hardware">
<label for="4-4-held-ptn-hardware">hardware</label>
<img class="shot-webapp" src="/assets/mseq/4-4-held-ptn.png" alt="The same three rows, each showing yellow-green pads at steps 1, 5, 9 and 13 with slate trails running behind them, a plain teal trig at step 8, and dark gaps at steps 4, 7, 12 and 16">
<img class="shot-hardware" src="/assets/mseq/hardware/4-4-held-ptn.jpg" alt="The same three rows, each showing yellow-green pads at steps 1, 5, 9 and 13 with slate trails running behind them, a plain teal trig at step 8, and dark gaps at steps 4, 7, 12 and 16, photographed on the hardware">
</figure>

*This is where held trigs earn their place. Each yellow-green pad starts a note and
the slate pads behind it are that note still sounding, so you can read the length
straight off the grid. Four held notes here, running 1 to 3, 5 to 6, 9 to 11 and 13
to 15, with a rest before each one and a plain teal trig at step 8 firing short in
among them. (The first note's start pad is under the playhead, which is why step 1
looks washed out rather than yellow-green.) That mix of long, short and silent is
most of what makes a line phrase rather than tick.*

**5. The same legato, from the row's play mode.** Hold **SOLO** on the
LaunchControl and press a row button.

<figure class="fig-pair">
<input type="radio" name="4-4-sustain" id="4-4-sustain-webapp" class="pick-webapp" checked>
<label for="4-4-sustain-webapp">webapp</label>
<input type="radio" name="4-4-sustain" id="4-4-sustain-hardware" class="pick-hardware">
<label for="4-4-sustain-hardware">hardware</label>
<img class="shot-webapp" src="/assets/mseq/4-4-sustain.png" alt="The four-trig chord again with an untouched grid, and the row buttons now blue">
<img class="shot-hardware" src="/assets/mseq/hardware/4-4-sustain.jpg" alt="The four-trig chord again with an untouched grid, and the row buttons now blue, photographed on the hardware">
</figure>

*Blue row buttons are legato, and the grid is back to the plain four trigs. Each
note is stretched to reach the next one, which sounds the same as holding every
trig across to its neighbour. The difference is where the decision lives: held
trigs are written into the pattern and travel with it, legato is a property of the
row that you can switch off in a second.*

**6. A drone, when you want the chord to just sit there.** Hold **MUTE** and
press a row button.

<figure class="fig-pair">
<input type="radio" name="4-4-drone" id="4-4-drone-webapp" class="pick-webapp" checked>
<label for="4-4-drone-webapp">webapp</label>
<input type="radio" name="4-4-drone" id="4-4-drone-hardware" class="pick-hardware">
<label for="4-4-drone-hardware">hardware</label>
<img class="shot-webapp" src="/assets/mseq/4-4-drone.png" alt="The same chord and grid, with the row buttons now green">
<img class="shot-hardware" src="/assets/mseq/hardware/4-4-drone.jpg" alt="The same chord and grid, with the row buttons now green, photographed on the hardware">
</figure>

*Green row buttons are drone. One note fires and is held indefinitely, and the
trigs are ignored completely while it lasts, which is why the grid looks identical
to the figure above and sounds nothing like it. Useful for a pad you want to hold
under a section, and instant to leave.*

So: **duty** for the length of one hit, **held trigs** for a shape you want to keep,
**legato** for the same effect as a switch, and **drone** to leave the pattern out of
it. Row play modes are covered on their own in
[Mutes and row states](/documentation/MSEQ/mutes).

## Modulo Division Reference

The 16-bar cycle counts bars 0–15. Mod and InvMod conditions evaluate at the bar level (not the step level):

| Status | Fires on bars | Mnemonic |
|--------|---------------|----------|
| <span style="display:inline-block;inline-size:.95em;block-size:.95em;background:#e3aed7;border:solid 1px rgba(219,219,219,0.5);vertical-align:-.12em;margin-inline-end:.55em"></span>MOD1 | 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14 | Every other bar (even) |
| <span style="display:inline-block;inline-size:.95em;block-size:.95em;background:#e7d8fd;border:solid 1px rgba(219,219,219,0.5);vertical-align:-.12em;margin-inline-end:.55em"></span>MOD2 | 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13, 15 | Every other bar (odd) |
| <span style="display:inline-block;inline-size:.95em;block-size:.95em;background:#77c5ff;border:solid 1px rgba(219,219,219,0.5);vertical-align:-.12em;margin-inline-end:.55em"></span>MOD4 | 3, 7, 11, 15 | Every 4th bar |
| <span style="display:inline-block;inline-size:.95em;block-size:.95em;background:#609dff;border:solid 1px rgba(219,219,219,0.5);vertical-align:-.12em;margin-inline-end:.55em"></span>MOD8 | 7, 15 | Every 8th bar |
| <span style="display:inline-block;inline-size:.95em;block-size:.95em;background:#013ac0;border:solid 1px rgba(219,219,219,0.5);vertical-align:-.12em;margin-inline-end:.55em"></span>MOD16 | 15 | Once per cycle |
| <span style="display:inline-block;inline-size:.95em;block-size:.95em;background:#c29d0d;border:solid 1px rgba(219,219,219,0.5);vertical-align:-.12em;margin-inline-end:.55em"></span>INVMOD4 | All except 3, 7, 11, 15 | 3 out of 4 bars |
| <span style="display:inline-block;inline-size:.95em;block-size:.95em;background:#822c08;border:solid 1px rgba(219,219,219,0.5);vertical-align:-.12em;margin-inline-end:.55em"></span>INVMOD8 | All except 7, 15 | 7 out of 8 bars |
| <span style="display:inline-block;inline-size:.95em;block-size:.95em;background:#820610;border:solid 1px rgba(219,219,219,0.5);vertical-align:-.12em;margin-inline-end:.55em"></span>INVMOD16 | All except 15 | 15 out of 16 bars |
